Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 105, verse 1:

(Surat al-Fil)
Five verses, Meccan

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾

It is related that Abraha ibn al-Sabbah al-Ashram, the king of Yemen on behalf of Ashama al-Najashi, built a church in Sana'a and named it al-Qulays, and he wanted to divert the pilgrims to it. A man from the Banu Kinana went out and defecated in it at night, and this angered him.

It is also said: a group of Arabs lit a fire, and the wind carried it and it burned the church. So he swore that he would demolish the Ka'ba. He set out with the Abyssinians, and with him was an elephant named Mahmud, which was strong and huge, and eight others. It is said there were twelve, and it is said there were a thousand. When he reached near Makka, Abd al-Muttalib went out to him and offered him a third of the wealth of Tihama in return for his turning back, but he refused and arrayed his army, and he sent the elephant forward. Whenever they directed it toward the direction of the Haram it knelt and would not move, and whenever they directed it toward Yemen or any other direction it ran. Then Abraha seized two hundred camels belonging to Abd al-Muttalib, and he went out to them to recover them. He became great in the eyes of Abraha, for he was a tall and handsome man. It was said: this is the chief of Quraysh and the owner of the caravans of Makka. When he mentioned his need, [Abraha] said: "You have fallen from my eyes. I came to demolish the House which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, but a few camels taken from you have distracted you from it." He replied: "I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it from you." Then he returned and came to the House, took hold of its ring, and was saying:

"O God, a man defends his own property,
so defend Your sanctuary.
Let not their cross and their schemes
overcome Your scheme tomorrow.
If You leave them and our Ka'ba,
then do as You see fit."

And he was saying:
"O Lord, I do not hope for anyone but You;
O Lord, protect Your sanctuary from them."

Then he turned while supplicating, and behold, there was a bird coming from the direction of Yemen. He said: "By God, it is a strange bird; it is neither from Najd nor from Tihama." Each bird had a stone in its beak and two stones in its feet, larger than a lentil and smaller than a chickpea. It is related from Ibn Abbas that he saw some of them with Umm Hani, about a qafiz, speckled with red like Zafari onyx. The stone would fall on a man's head and come out of his anus, and on each stone was the name of the one it would fall upon. They perished on every road and watering place. Abraha was afflicted, and his fingers fell off, and he did not die until his chest split open from his heart. His vizier Abu Yaksum escaped with a bird circling above him until he reached the Najashi, and he related the story to him. When he finished it, a stone fell upon him and he dropped dead before him. It is related from Aisha, she said: "I saw the driver of the elephant and its keeper, both blind and crippled, begging for food."

Then in the verse there are questions:
The first: Why did He say "Have you not considered" when this event occurred a long time before the mission? The answer: The intended meaning of "seeing" is knowledge and reminder, and it indicates that the report of it is widely transmitted (mutawatir), so the knowledge obtained from it is necessary, equal in strength and clarity to sight. For this reason He said to others, in a manner of reproach: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 31]. It cannot be said: then why did He say ﴿Do you not know that God is able to do all things?﴾ [al-Baqara: 106]? We say: the difference is that what cannot be perceived is only described with knowledge, because of His power, whereas what can be perceived, such as the fleeing of the elephant, may be described with seeing.

The second question: Why did He say ﴿how your Lord dealt﴾ and not "what your Lord did"? The answer: Because things have essences, and they have modes (kayfiyyat), and by considering them one deduces their continuity. These modes are what the theologians call the "aspect of the proof" (wajh al-dalil), and deserving praise is attained only by seeing these modes, not by seeing the essences. For this reason He said: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We built it?﴾ [Qaf: 6]. There is no doubt that this event was indicative of the power, knowledge and wisdom of the Creator, and it was indicative of the nobility of Muhammad ﷺ. This is because our school holds that miracles may precede the time of the mission, as a foundation for his prophethood and a preparation for it. Therefore they said: a cloud used to shade him. But according to the Mu'tazila, this is not permissible, so they inevitably claimed that there must have been in that time a prophet (or an orator), such as Khalid ibn Sinan or Qus ibn Sa'ida. Then they said: it is not necessary that their existence be well known and reach the level of mass transmission, since it is possible that he was sent to a small group, so his report did not become famous.

Know that the story of the elephant is a very strong proof against the atheists, for they attributed the earthquakes, winds, thunderbolts and all other things through which God punished nations to weak causes. But this event is not subject to those excuses, for there is nothing in nature or in stratagems by which a bird carrying stones should approach and target one people rather than another and kill them. Nor can it be said that it is like the other weak reports, because between the Year of the Elephant and the sending of the Messenger there were only about forty-odd years, and on the day the Messenger recited this surah there remained in Makka a group who had witnessed that event; had the report been weak, they would have denied it to his face. Since this was not so, we know there is no ground for disputing it.

The third question: Why did He say "fa'ala" (did) and not "ja'ala" (made), "khalaqa" (created) or "amila" (worked)? The answer: Because "khalaqa" is used for initiating an act, and "ja'ala" for modes. He, exalted, said: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. "Amila" is used after deliberation, and "fa'ala" is general, so it is more appropriate, because He created the birds and changed the nature of the elephant from what it had been, and they asked Him to protect the House, and perhaps among them were some who deserved to be answered. Had He mentioned the three words, the speech would have been long, so He mentioned a word that encompasses all.

The fourth question: Why did He say "your Lord" and not "the Lord"? The answer: in several ways:

The first: It is as if He, exalted, said: When they witnessed this retribution and yet did not abandon the worship of idols, and you, O Muhammad, did not witness it but acknowledged thankfulness and obedience, then it is as though you are the one who saw that retribution. Therefore I have disassociated from them and chosen you over all. So I say: "your Lord," meaning I am yours and not theirs, but rather against them.

The second: It is as if He, exalted, said: I did that to the companions of the elephant only to honour you and to exalt your coming, for I was nurturing you before your people. How then would I abandon your nurturing after your emergence? In this there is good news for him, peace be upon him, that he will be victorious.

The fifth question: His saying ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt...﴾ is stated in the context of wonder, yet these things in relation to the power of God, exalted, are not wondrous. So what is the reason for this wonder? The answer: in several ways:

The first: The Ka'ba is a follower of Muhammad ﷺ, because knowledge is conveyed without a mosque, but there is no mosque without a scholar. The scholar is the pearl and the mosque is the shell. Then the Messenger, who is the pearl, was mocked and slandered by al-Walid until his heart was constricted. It is as if He, exalted, says: The great king, when he reviled the mosque, I defeated and destroyed him; so whoever reviles you, when you are the goal of all, shall I not destroy and annihilate him? Indeed, this is wondrous!

The second: The Ka'ba is the qibla of your prayer, and your heart is the qibla of your knowledge. Then I protected the qibla of your action from enemies; shall we not strive to protect the qibla of your religion from sins and disobedience?

The sixth question: Why did He say ﴿the companions of the elephant﴾ and not "the lords of the elephant" or "the owners of the elephant"? The answer: Because the companion is of the same kind, so His saying ﴿the companions of the elephant﴾ indicates that those people were of the same kind as the elephant in brutishness, lack of understanding and reason. Indeed, there is a subtle point in it: when companionship occurs between two persons, it is said of the lesser that he is the companion of the greater, but it is not said of the greater that he is the companion of the lesser. For this reason, those who accompanied the Messenger, peace be upon him, are called the Sahaba (Companions). So His saying ﴿the companions of the elephant﴾ indicates that those people were of lesser condition and of lower rank than the elephant, and this is what is meant by His saying, exalted: ﴿Rather, they are more astray﴾ [al-A'raf: 179]. What confirms this is that whenever they directed the elephant toward the direction of

the Ka'ba, it would turn away from it and flee from it, as if it were saying: there is no obedience to a created being in disobedience to the Creator. "My resolve is praiseworthy, so I will not abandon it." Yet they did not abandon that wicked resolve. This indicates that the elephant was in a better state than they were.

The seventh question: Did not the unbelievers of Quraysh fill the Ka'ba with idols from ancient times? Without doubt, that was more abhorrent than destroying the walls of the Ka'ba. Why then did God send punishment upon the one who intended destruction, and did not send punishment upon those who filled it with idols?

The answer: Because placing idols in it is a transgression upon the right of God, exalted, while destroying it is a transgression upon the right of creatures. A parallel to this is the highwayman, and the rebel and the murderer, who are executed even though they are Muslims; and an old man, a blind man, a monk in his hermitage, and a woman are not killed, even if they are unbelievers, because their harm does not extend to creatures.

The eighth question: What is the view on the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of this verse? The answer: al-Zajjaj said: "kayfa" is in the accusative position governed by a verb other than "alam tara", because "kayfa" is one of the interrogative particles.

**Know** that He, exalted is He, mentioned what He did to them, saying: ﴿Did He not make their plot go astray?﴾ There are several issues concerning this.

**The first issue:** Know that *al-kayd* (plotting, scheming) is an action intended to harm another secretly. If it is said: why did He call it a plot when its matter was apparent, since [Abraha] openly declared that he would demolish the House? We say: Yes, but what was in his heart was worse than what he displayed, for he harbored envy toward the Arabs, and he wanted to transfer the honor that came to them, from the Ka'bah, from them and from their land, to himself and to his own city.

**The second issue:** The Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazila, a rationalist theological school) said: the attribution of the plot to them is evidence that He, exalted is He, does not approve of what is ugly, for if He approved of it He would have attributed it to Himself, as in His saying: "Fasting is for Me." The answer: it is established in the science of grammar (*'ilm al-nahw*) that even the slightest cause suffices for the propriety of an idiomatic attribution (*idafah*). So why would the fact that the act conformed to their own will and choice not suffice for the propriety of this attribution?

**The third issue:** ﴿in tadlil﴾ means "in loss and nullification." It is said: *dallala kaydahu* when one makes his plot go astray, i.e., makes it lost and wasted. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾ [Ghafir: 50]. It was said to Imru' al-Qays: "the astray king" (*al-malik al-dalil*), because he caused his father's kingdom to go astray, i.e., wasted it. The meaning is that they first plotted against the House by building the *Qulays* (a church in Yemen), intending to begin their affair by diverting the faces of the pilgrims toward it; so He made their plot go astray by bringing fire upon it. Then they plotted against it a second time by intending to demolish it, so He made it go astray by sending the birds against them. The meaning of the particle of place (*harf al-zarf*, here *fi*) is as when one says: "So-and-so's striving is in error," meaning that his striving had become evident to every intelligent person as being error and mistake.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He sent against them birds in flocks﴾. There are issues concerning this:

**The first question:** Why did He say *tayran* (birds) in indefinite form? The answer: either it is for belittling, for whatever is smaller, the work of God is more wondrous and greater; or it is for magnification, as if He were saying: "birds, and what birds! They pelted with small stones and did not miss the mark."

**The second question:** What are *ababil*? The answer: As for the lexicographers, Abu 'Ubaydah said: *ababil* means groups in dispersion. It is said: "The horses came *ababil ababil*," from here and from there. Does this word have a singular or not? There are two views:

The first, which is the view of al-Akhfash and al-Farra': it has no singular, and it is like *al-shamatit* and *al-'abadid*, which have no singular.

The second: it does have a singular. Then, on this view, they mentioned three opinions:

The first: Abu Ja'far al-Ru'asi, who was trustworthy and reliable, claimed that he heard its singular to be *ibbalah*, and in their proverbs: "a handful upon a bundle" (*dighth 'ala ibbalah*), and it is the large bundle. The group of birds in their arrangement was named *ibbalah*.

The second: al-Kisa'i said: "I used to hear the grammarians say: *ibul* and *ababil*, like *'ujul* and *'ajajil*."

The third: al-Farra' said: "If someone said the singular of *ababil* is *iyballah*, it would be correct, just as one says *dinar* and *danaanir*."

**The third question:** What was the description of those birds? The answer: Ibn Sirin narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: they were birds that had snouts like the snouts of elephants and talons like the talons of dogs. 'Ata' narrated from him, who said: they were black birds that came from the direction of the sea, in groups after groups. Perhaps the reason is that they were sent against a people whose outward appearance was dark in color and whose inner being was dark with the darkness of disbelief and disobedience. And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: they were small and white. Perhaps the reason is that the darkness of disbelief was routed by them, and whiteness is the opposite of blackness. It was also said: they were green and had heads like the heads of beasts of prey. I say: since they came in flocks, perhaps each flock was of a different form, so each person described what he saw. It was also said: they were piebald, like swallows.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Striking them with stones of baked clay﴾. And in this are several issues:

The first issue: Abu Haywa recited "yarmīhim" (He strikes them), meaning Allah, or the birds, because it is a collective noun in the masculine gender, and it is only made feminine according to meaning.

The second issue: They mentioned several views regarding the manner of the striking:

The first of them: Muqatil said: Every bird carried three stones, one in its beak and two in its feet, each one killing a man, and on each stone was written the name of its owner. Whenever a stone fell upon a place, it came out from the other side, and if it fell upon his head, it came out from his anus.

The second of them: Ikrimah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: When Allah sent the stones upon the companions of the elephant, no stone fell upon any of them except that its skin blistered and smallpox erupted on it. This is also the view of Saʿid ibn Jubayr. Those stones were, the smallest of them like a lentil, and the largest of them like a chickpea.

Know that some people denied this and said: If we permit that there could be in stones the size of a lentil such weight that it could pass through a man's head and emerge from beneath him, then we would permit that a great mountain be empty of weight and be of the weight of a bran husk, and that removes the certainty of observed things. For whenever that is permitted, it would be permissible that there be suns and moons in our presence which we do not see, and that perception occur in the eye of the blind so that he is in the east and sees a patch of land in Andalusia. All of that is impossible. Know that this is permissible according to our school, except that custom has it that such things do not occur.

The third issue: They mentioned several views regarding "sijjīl":

The first of them: That sijjīl is, as it were, a designation for the register in which the punishment of the disbelievers was written, just as Sijjin is a designation for the register of their deeds. It is as if it were said: with stones from among the punishment written and recorded. Its derivation is from al-ijjāl, which means sending, and from it comes al-sijjil, the bucket full of water. That book was named by this name because the punishment was written in it, and the punishment is described as being sent, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He sent upon them birds in flocks﴾ and His saying: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 133]. So His saying: ﴿of sijjīl﴾ means: of what Allah wrote in that book.

The second: Ibn ʿAbbas said: sijjīl means "sankak and kil", meaning some of it is stone and some of it is clay.

The third: Abu ʿUbayda said: sijjīl means "the strong."

The fourth: Sijjīl is the name of the lowest heaven.

The fifth: Sijjīl is stones from Hell, for sijjīl is one of the names of Hell, and the nūn was replaced with the lām.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So He made them like eaten stalks﴾, there are several issues.

The first issue: They have mentioned various interpretations of al-'asf (the stalk/chaff, lit. the leaves or husk of grain), which we have mentioned in His saying: ﴿And the grain having husk (dhu al-'asf)﴾ [al-Rahman: 12]. They have mentioned several views here:

One of them: It is the leaves of the crop that remain in the field after the harvest, which the winds blow about and which the livestock then eat.

Second: Abu Muslim said: al-'asf is straw (tibn), due to His saying: ﴿with husk and the basil (dhu al-'asf wa al-rayhan)﴾ [al-Rahman: 12], because the wind blows it away at the time of threshing, separating it from the grain. When it has been eaten, it is ruined, with no return and no strength in it.

Third: al-Farra' said: it is the tips of the crop before it has ripened into the ear (sunbul).

Fourth: It is the grain whose kernel has been eaten while its husk remains.

The second issue: They have mentioned various interpretations of al-ma'kul (eaten):

One of them: That it is what has been eaten. On this view there are two possibilities:

The first: The meaning is like a crop and straw that animals have eaten, then expelled as dung, which then dries and its parts scatter. He likened the disintegration of their joints to the scattering of the parts of dung, except that the expression about it came in the manner dictated by the etiquette of the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿They both used to eat food﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 75]. This is the view of Muqatil, Qatadah and 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second possibility: On this view, the comparison is with the leaves of the crop when the eating-worm (al-akkal) falls upon it, which is when worms eat it.

The second view on the interpretation of His saying "ma'kul": that He made them like a crop whose grain has been eaten while its straw remains. On this reckoning the meaning is: "like stalks eaten of their grain," just as one says: "So-and-so is handsome," meaning handsome of face. So "ma'kul" is applied to the stalk because its grain has been eaten, since this meaning is known. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The third view on the interpretation: that the meaning of "ma'kul" is that it is something that is eaten, i.e., the animals eat it. It is said: everything fit for eating is ma'kul. The meaning is: He made them like straw that the animals eat. This is the view of 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak.

The third issue: Some have said: al-Hajjaj demolished the Ka'bah, and nothing of that happened. This indicates that the story of the Elephant was not in this manner. And even if it was thus, the cause of that event was another matter besides the glorification of the Ka'bah. The answer: We have explained that this occurred as a preparatory sign (irhas) for the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the irhas is only needed before his coming. As for after his coming and the confirmation of his prophethood by decisive proofs, there is no need for any of that. And Allah, Glorified and Exalted, knows best and is most wise. And may Allah bless our master Muhammad, and his family and companions, and grant them peace.
